content: Epilepsy affects approximately 1% of the global population, and up to 30% of these individuals continue to experience seizures despite treatment with antiepileptic drugs. Clobazam, a 1,5-benzodiazepine, is frequently used as an add-on therapy for patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. This review is an updated version of the original Cochrane Review published in 2008 and evaluates the most recent evidence regarding the use of clobazam as an adjunctive treatment for drug-resistant epilepsy. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy, effectiveness, and tolerability of clobazam as an add-on therapy for drug-resistant generalized-onset and focal-onset seizures, with or without secondary generalization, in both adults and children. For the latest update, a comprehensive search of multiple databases was conducted on October 9, 2018. These databases included the Cochrane Register of Studies (CRS Web), which encompasses the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), as well as Medline (Ovid), ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). Previous updates also included searches in SCOPUS, DARE, and BIOSIS Previews, but these were deemed unnecessary for the current review due to changes in database coverage and relevance. The review included randomized trials of add-on clobazam therapy with adequate allocation concealment methods. Participants were required to have drug-resistant focal or generalized-onset seizures, and the minimum treatment duration was eight weeks. Two independent reviewers selected the trials and extracted relevant data. The outcomes assessed included a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency, seizure freedom, treatment withdrawal, and adverse events. Four double-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over studies involving 197 participants were included in the review. However, all four studies were assessed as having an unclear risk of bias due to insufficient methodological details. Significant heterogeneity in study design and outcome measures prevented the data from being pooled into a meta-analysis. Instead, the findings were summarized narratively. Two of the studies reported a 50% or greater reduction in seizure frequency. In these studies, 57.7% and 52.4% of participants receiving add-on clobazam achieved this level of seizure reduction. However, the evidence was of very low quality, and the potential for publication bias was noted (2 RCTs, n = 47). Seizure freedom was reported in three studies, with 27 out of 175 participants achieving seizure freedom during clobazam treatment. In contrast, two studies explicitly stated that no participants receiving placebo achieved seizure freedom (3 RCTs, n = 175, very low-quality evidence). All four studies reported on treatment withdrawal. There was a slightly higher rate of treatment withdrawal among participants receiving clobazam compared to placebo, but the overall incidence remained low (4 RCTs, n = 197, very low-quality evidence). Adverse events were described in two studies, with 36% and 85% of participants experiencing one or more adverse events while on clobazam. The most frequently reported adverse event was drowsiness. The authors concluded that clobazam as an add-on therapy may reduce seizure frequency, particularly in focal-onset seizures. However, this conclusion is based on very low-quality evidence from studies with unclear risk of bias. It remains uncertain which patient populations would derive the most benefit from clobazam or the optimal duration of treatment. To better inform clinical practice, a large-scale, randomized controlled trial with a longer follow-up period and inclusion of subgroups with different seizure types is necessary.
